hint: Use the Web Audio API to synthesize piano notes using oscillators. The Tone.js library provides a higher-level API for musical synthesis.
approach: Visual piano: 2 octaves, clickable keys. Audio: Tone.js sampler using high-quality piano samples (or oscillator synthesis). Lessons: (1) Notes and positions, (2) Major scales (highlight scale notes on keyboard), (3) Minor scales, (4) Intervals (play two notes, label the interval), (5) Chords (show and play major/minor/7th chords). Interactive exercises: hear a chord, identify it; hear an interval, name it. Ear training mode: play mystery notes, user identifies by clicking. Chord progression player: play common progressions in any key. Quiz with score tracking. Progress saved locally.

title: Build a Personalized News Aggregator
description: A news reader wants a custom feed that combines sources they trust, filtered by topics they care about, with no algorithm manipulation.
task: Design a personalized news reader that fetches from RSS feeds and topic APIs. How would you score articles for relevance without a recommendation algorithm?
hint: Let users explicitly define interests as keywords. Score articles by keyword match in title/summary. Fully transparent scoring.
approach: Setup: user adds RSS feed URLs + topic keywords they care about. Fetch: poll RSS feeds every 30min (background sync). Score: for each article, count keyword matches in title (weight 3) + summary (weight 1). Sort by score × recency. Display: article cards with source, title, summary, match score, read time. Mark as read (hidden by default). Save for later. Filter by source or topic. No black-box algorithm — user sees exactly why an article ranked high. OPML import for bulk feed addition. Dark mode. Export reading list.

title: Create a Pixel Art Editor
description: An indie game developer wants a lightweight browser-based pixel art editor for creating game sprites.
task: Design a pixel art editor with drawing tools, color palette, and sprite animation. How would you handle zoom and the canvas grid efficiently?
hint: Use a canvas where each pixel is a fixed number of screen pixels (e.g., 16px each at 100% zoom). Track pixel colors in a 2D array.
approach: Canvas: 32x32 or 64x64 grid, each cell = 8-16px screen pixels (zoom-dependent). Data: 2D array of color values. Tools: pencil (set color on click/drag), eraser, fill bucket (flood fill BFS), line, rectangle, circle, eyedropper. Color palette: 16 preset colors + custom color picker + recently used. Layers: multiple layers with opacity. Animation frames: create multiple frames, preview as animation at configurable FPS. Undo/redo stack. Zoom: 1x to 16x. Export: PNG sprite sheet, individual frames, or GIF animation. Import existing PNG to edit. Onion skin mode (see previous frame transparently).

title: Design a Feedback Collection System
description: A product team wants to collect structured user feedback at key moments without annoying users with surveys.
task: Design an in-app feedback collection system. How would you decide when to ask for feedback? How would you prevent survey fatigue?
hint: Trigger feedback requests based on user events (completed a key action, session length > 5min) not time-based popups. Limit to once per 30 days per user.
approach: Trigger rules: after user completes a key action (exported a file, finished an onboarding, made first purchase), after 5+ sessions (engaged user), never during checkout or critical flows. Fatigue prevention: 30-day cooldown per user, max 3 surveys per month per user. Survey types: NPS (0-10 would you recommend), CSAT (1-5 satisfaction), CES (1-7 effort), micro-survey (1 specific question). Non-blocking UI: slide-in from corner, dismissible, can snooze. Follow-up: if rating < 7, show open text box for details. Analytics dashboard: NPS trend over time, segmentation by feature/cohort, alert on score drop.

title: Create a Browser-Based SSH Client
description: A developer wants to access their Linux servers through the browser without installing an SSH client.
task: Design a web-based SSH client. Since browsers can't make direct TCP connections, how would you bridge the WebSocket-to-SSH gap?
hint: Use a WebSocket proxy server (websockify or a custom Node.js proxy) that bridges WebSocket connections to SSH, then render the terminal with xterm.js.
approach: Architecture: browser (xterm.js) ↔ WebSocket ↔ proxy server (Node.js + ssh2 library) ↔ SSH server. Frontend: xterm.js terminal with full ANSI support, keyboard shortcuts. Connection modal: host, port, username, password or SSH key upload. Proxy: authenticates the WebSocket connection, then opens SSH connection on behalf of the browser. Security: proxy must authenticate users before allowing SSH connections. Multiple tabs: each SSH session gets its own WebSocket connection. Saved connections: store in localStorage (never store passwords). SFTP file browser panel. Terminal sharing (view-only link for pair debugging).

title: Design a Typing Practice for Code
description: A developer wants to practice typing code faster using real code snippets from popular open source projects.
task: Build a code typing practice app that presents real code snippets and measures WPM, accuracy, and highlights common mistake patterns.
hint: Use GitHub's API to fetch actual code from popular repositories as practice material. Handle special characters and indentation carefully.
approach: Snippet sources: GitHub API fetches real code from popular repos (react, linux kernel, numpy). Filter by language selection (JavaScript, Python, Go). Snippet display: monospace font, syntax highlighted. Typing: compare typed character to expected, highlight correct (green) vs wrong (red). Metrics: WPM (calculated real-time), accuracy %, error count by character/key. After session: heatmap of most-missed keys, line chart of WPM over time. Difficulty levels: filter by line length and character complexity. Daily challenge: same snippet for all users that day. Personal records tracking. Pause/resume supported.

title: Build a Spreadsheet Collaboration Tool
description: A small team needs a simple shared spreadsheet for collaborative data entry without a Google Workspace subscription.
task: Design a basic real-time collaborative spreadsheet. How would you handle concurrent edits to the same cell? How would you store and sync the grid data?
hint: Use Operational Transformation or Last-Write-Wins with timestamps for concurrent edits. Show other users' cursors in their selected cells.
approach: Grid: 2D array of {value, formula, format}. Cell editing: double-click to enter edit mode, Enter/Tab to move. Formula support: =SUM(A1:A10), =AVERAGE(), basic arithmetic. Real-time sync: WebSocket broadcasts cell changes {row, col, value, userId}. Conflict: last-write-wins with timestamp, show conflict indicator on cell. Multi-user cursors: show colored selection boxes for each connected user with their name. Cell formatting: bold, italic, background color, text alignment. Column resize, row resize. CSV import/export. Undo/redo per user. Sheet tabs (multiple sheets per document). Permissions: read-only link vs edit link.

title: Create a Developer Changelog Generator
description: An open source maintainer wants to auto-generate release notes from git commits and PR descriptions.
task: Design a changelog generator that reads git history and creates user-friendly release notes. How would you filter technical commits from user-facing changes?
hint: Use conventional commit types (feat, fix, docs) to categorize changes. Send the categorized list to an LLM to rewrite in user-friendly language.
approach: Input: git log between two tags. Parse conventional commits: feat, fix, perf, breaking. Filter out: chore, test, refactor, docs (internal). For each PR: fetch description from GitHub API. Send categorized changes to LLM: 'Rewrite these technical git commits as a user-friendly changelog for version X.Y.Z. Group by: New Features, Bug Fixes, Performance Improvements, Breaking Changes. Use clear non-technical language.' Output: Markdown changelog. Preview before publishing. Auto-create GitHub release with the notes. Link each changelog item to its PR. Detect breaking changes from BREAKING CHANGE footer.

title: Design a Data Privacy Dashboard
description: A privacy-conscious user wants to see all the personal data apps have collected about them and request deletions.
task: Design a data privacy management dashboard. How would you help users discover what data companies have, and generate GDPR/CCPA deletion requests?
hint: Most companies have a data export API or GDPR request email. Generate legal deletion request emails personalized to each company's process.
approach: Company database: 200+ major services with their data request URLs/emails and processes (Google Takeout, Facebook Download, etc). User profile: which services they use (let them check from a list). For each service: show what data category they typically collect (location, purchases, browsing, contacts). Generate deletion requests: create a customized email for each service following their required format (some need specific subject lines). Track request status: sent, acknowledged, completed. Calendar reminders for follow-ups (companies have 30 days to respond). Know your rights section for GDPR/CCPA/DPDPA. Bulk request option.

title: Build a Rate Limiter Simulator
description: A backend developer wants to visually demonstrate different rate limiting algorithms to their team.
task: Design an interactive visualization of rate limiting algorithms (Token Bucket, Sliding Window, Fixed Window, Leaky Bucket). How would you show the algorithms accepting or rejecting requests in real-time?
hint: Animate a 'bucket' filling with tokens or a sliding window moving over a timeline. Show each request as a colored dot — green for accepted, red for rejected.
approach: Algorithm selector: Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, Fixed Window, Sliding Window. Parameter controls: rate, capacity, window size. Request generator: 'fire' requests at a slider-controlled rate or click manually. Animation: Token Bucket shows a bucket with token circles, consumed on each accepted request, refilled at set rate. Fixed Window shows a counter resetting at window boundaries. Sliding Window shows a moving time bar. Each request: green dot on success, red X on rejection. Stats: accepted/rejected ratio, bursting behavior demonstration. Code snippet showing each algorithm's implementation beside the animation. Side-by-side comparison mode.

title: Create a Voice-Controlled To-Do List
description: A hands-free user wants to add tasks, mark them done, and query their task list using only voice commands.
task: Design a voice-controlled task management app. How would you parse natural language voice commands into task actions? How would you give audio feedback?
hint: Use Web Speech API for both recognition and speech synthesis. Use an LLM to parse intent from natural language commands.
approach: Wake word: 'Hey Tasks' activates listening (or hold-to-talk button). Commands (parsed by LLM): 'Add buy groceries tomorrow' → {action:'add', task:'buy groceries', dueDate:tomorrow}. 'Mark buy groceries done' → {action:'complete', task:'buy groceries'}. 'What's on my list' → read all tasks aloud. 'Clear completed tasks' → delete done items. Text-to-speech feedback: 'Added: buy groceries, due tomorrow.' Visual display: current task list updates in real-time. Voice confirmation for destructive actions. Priority: 'Urgent: call the doctor'. Repeat unclear commands: 'I didn't catch that, please try again.'

title: Design a Commit History Storyteller
description: A developer wants to present the evolution of a project to new team members as a narrative story, not a raw git log.
task: Build a tool that turns a git repository's commit history into a narrative story of the project's evolution. How would you group commits into meaningful chapters?
hint: Cluster commits by time periods and by topic (using commit messages and changed files). Use an LLM to write each chapter's narrative.
approach: Fetch git log with full commit messages, dates, and changed files. Clustering: group commits into chapters by (1) time period (months/quarters) and (2) semantic similarity (group feature development together). For each chapter: list top commits, changed files, contributors. LLM prompt: 'Write a 2-3 paragraph narrative for this phase of project development. Describe what the team built, what challenges they faced (based on bug-fix commits), and the overall direction.' Output: interactive timeline with expandable chapters. Contributors hall of fame. Key milestones extracted. Export as PDF or presentation slides.

title: Build an Automated Status Page
description: A SaaS startup needs a public status page that automatically reflects service health without manual updates.
task: Design an automated status page system that monitors service health and communicates incidents to users. How would you detect incidents automatically?
hint: Run health checks every minute from multiple regions. Use a state machine (operational → degraded → outage → resolved) to automatically update status.
approach: Health checks: CRON every 60s hits /health endpoint of each service from 3+ regions. Success criteria: HTTP 200 + response time < 2s. State machine: 1 failure → degraded, 3 consecutive failures → outage, 3 consecutive successes → operational. Status page: current status per service (API, Database, CDN), 90-day uptime percentage, current incidents with timeline. Subscriber notifications: email/SMS/Slack on status change. Incident updates: internal admin can add manual updates during incidents. Maintenance windows: scheduled downtime shown in advance. SLA calculator: actual uptime vs committed SLA. Historical incident reports exportable.

title: Create a CSS Component Library Builder
description: A design team wants to create their own CSS component library with documented, copy-paste-ready components.
task: Design a tool for building and documenting a CSS component library. How would you let teams customize design tokens while keeping components consistent?
hint: Use CSS custom properties for all design tokens. Provide a visual token editor that updates all components in real-time.
approach: Design tokens: colors (primary, secondary, accent, neutral scale), typography (font family, size scale, weights), spacing scale, border radius, shadows. Token editor: visual controls (color picker, sliders) that update CSS custom properties. Component catalog: buttons (variants, sizes, states), inputs, cards, modals, badges, alerts. Each component shows: live preview with current tokens, HTML/CSS code to copy, accessibility notes, usage guidelines. Export: CSS file with all tokens + components, or separate files. Dark mode preview toggle. Multiple brand themes. Embed as iframe in any documentation site.

title: Build a Live Code Sharing Platform
description: A teacher wants to share code with students during a live session and see all their screens simultaneously.
task: Design a live coding session platform for teaching. How would you sync code between teacher and all students in real-time? How would you handle 50+ simultaneous connections?
hint: Use WebSockets with a room-based pub/sub model. The teacher is the 'broadcaster', students are 'subscribers'. Use operational transformation for conflict-free edits.
approach: Teacher creates room → gets shareable URL. Students join and see teacher's code in real-time (read-only mode). Teacher can optionally unlock student editing (collaborative mode). WebSocket architecture: each room has a channel. Teacher edits → server broadcasts diffs to all students. Code editor: Monaco with syntax highlighting. Student view: each student has their own editor, teacher can click any student's name to view their code on teacher's screen. Live assessment: teacher sets a challenge, timer starts, students code solutions, teacher sees all simultaneously. Run code: execute in sandbox, show output. Raise hand feature for questions.

title: Design a Privacy-First Analytics Tool
description: A website owner wants basic analytics (pageviews, bounce rate, traffic sources) without using Google Analytics and tracking cookies.
task: Design a cookie-free, privacy-first analytics system. How would you identify unique visitors without cookies? How would you stay GDPR compliant?
hint: Use a daily hash of IP + User-Agent for unique visitor estimation. No persistent tracking, no cross-site tracking, no PII storage.
approach: Tracking: 1-2KB JavaScript snippet sends page view events. Unique visitors: daily hash of IP+UserAgent+salt (changes daily → no persistent tracking). No cookies. Data collected: URL, referrer, country (from IP, then IP discarded), device type, browser, screen size. No PII ever stored. Dashboard: unique visitors, pageviews, bounce rate, top pages, traffic sources, device breakdown, country map. Lightweight: single serverless function receives events, stores in SQLite or PostgreSQL. Comparison mode: this week vs last week. No sampling for small sites. Self-hostable. 100% GDPR compliant without consent banner.

title: Create a Schema-to-UI Generator
description: A developer wants to paste a JSON schema or database table definition and get a working React form generated automatically.
task: Design a tool that converts JSON Schema or SQL CREATE TABLE statements into a complete React form with validation. How would you infer UI patterns from data types?
hint: Use an LLM to generate the React component from the schema. Map types: string→text, boolean→checkbox, enum→select, date→datepicker.
approach: Input: JSON Schema or SQL CREATE TABLE. Parse: extract fields, types, constraints (required, minLength, pattern, enum). Type-to-component mapping: string→<input type=text>, email→email input with pattern, integer→number input with min/max, boolean→checkbox, enum→<select>, date→date picker, text (long)→textarea, array→multi-select or tag input. Validation: generate Zod or Yup schema from constraints. Output: complete React component with useState, validation, and submit handler. LLM enhancement: infer better labels and placeholder text from field names. Preview the generated form. Export as .tsx file.

title: Build a Personal Knowledge Base
description: A researcher wants a connected note-taking system where ideas link to each other like a wiki, not a linear list.
task: Design a networked knowledge base (like Roam Research or Obsidian) with bidirectional links and a graph visualization. How would you implement [[wiki-style links]] between notes?
hint: Parse [[Note Name]] syntax in note content. Build a bidirectional link index: when Note A links to Note B, Note B shows A in its backlinks panel.
approach: Notes stored as markdown files (or JSON). Editor: CodeMirror with [[autocomplete]] for note titles. Link parsing: on save, extract all [[links]], update bidirectional index. Graph view: D3 force-directed graph, nodes = notes, edges = links. Click node → open note. Note view: content area + backlinks panel (which notes link here). Tag system: #tags create implicit links. Full-text search across all notes. Daily notes: auto-create today's note as a journal. Unlinked references: find mentions of a note's title that aren't linked yet. Export as Obsidian vault (compatible format). Import from Notion or Roam.

title: Create a Distributed Systems Fault Simulator
description: An engineering team wants to practice incident response by simulating common distributed systems failures.
task: Design an interactive distributed systems simulator that visualizes node failures, network partitions, and cascading failures. How would you make it educational?
hint: Simulate a cluster of nodes as circles on screen. Let users inject failures and watch how the system responds — which nodes fail, which recover, what data is lost.
approach: Visual: cluster of 5-10 nodes as circles. States: healthy (green), degraded (yellow), failed (red), recovering (blue). Connections between nodes shown as lines (thick = high traffic, broken = partitioned). Fault injection: kill a node, slow a link, partition the network (cut all links between two groups). System types: leader-election, eventually-consistent DB, consensus (Raft). Metrics: request success rate, leader election time, data consistency score. Scenario presets: 'Majority partition', 'Network brownout', 'Rolling restart'. Step-by-step mode: advance time manually. Post-mortem: timeline of what happened and why. Learning mode: narrated explanations of what each failure demonstrates.

title: Build a Competitive Analysis Board
description: A product manager wants a structured way to track competitor features, pricing, and positioning over time.
task: Design a competitive intelligence dashboard. How would you structure the comparison matrix? How would AI help with tracking competitor changes?
hint: Use a feature matrix (rows = features, columns = competitors) with color-coded cells. AI can monitor competitor pages and flag changes.
approach: Feature matrix: rows = features/capabilities, columns = your product + competitors. Cell values: ✅ (has it), ❌ (no), 🔶 (partial), or text description. Score each competitor overall automatically from the matrix. Pricing table: separate section comparing pricing tiers. Positioning radar chart: 5-6 dimensions (ease of use, features, price, support, scalability). AI monitoring: save competitor website URLs, CRON runs weekly to check for changes, AI summarizes what changed (new features page, pricing change, new case studies). Change history: timeline of when each competitor made moves. Share report as PDF. Tag features by category. Export to PowerPoint.

title: Design a Keyboard Shortcut Discovery Tool
description: Users of a complex app forget keyboard shortcuts. The tool should surface relevant shortcuts based on what the user is currently doing.
task: Design an intelligent shortcut discovery system. How would you show relevant shortcuts contextually rather than dumping a huge table on users?
hint: Track which UI section the user is in and which actions they perform with the mouse. Show shortcuts for mouse actions they performed in the last 30 seconds.
approach: Shortcut registry: map {action, shortcut, context} for all app shortcuts. Context detection: which panel is focused (editor, sidebar, modal). Shortcut discovery panel: triggered by ? key. Instead of showing all shortcuts, show: (1) Shortcuts for actions user just did with mouse (if you clicked Bold button, show Cmd+B), (2) Top 5 most-used shortcuts for current context. Shortcut coach mode: when user clicks a button that has a shortcut, show a brief tooltip 'Tip: use Cmd+B'. Dismiss after user uses the shortcut 3 times. Progressive disclosure: show beginner shortcuts first, advanced after engagement. Custom shortcuts: let power users remap.

title: Build a Tech Debt Visualizer
description: An engineering manager wants to quantify and visualize technical debt across a codebase to make the business case for refactoring.
task: Design a tech debt tracking and visualization system. How would you quantify debt? How would you help teams prioritize which debt to pay down first?
hint: Combine static code metrics (complexity, duplication, test coverage) with business metrics (change frequency, bug rate) to prioritize high-risk debt.
approach: Data sources: (1) Code analysis: cyclomatic complexity, code duplication %, test coverage per file (from coverage reports). (2) Git history: change frequency per file/module over last 6 months. (3) Bug tracker: bugs filed per module. Debt score: high complexity + high change frequency + low test coverage = highest priority debt. Visualization: treemap where size=code size, color=debt score (green to red). Drill into modules. Debt register: curated list of known debt items with effort estimate and business impact. ROI calculator: estimated hours saved per quarter if debt fixed. Prioritization matrix: effort vs impact bubble chart. Trend over time: is debt growing or shrinking?
